evidence_i_missed: City of Edmonton Statements of Significance for the Hardisty Residence (10549 126 Street NW) and the Griffith Residence (12526 109A Avenue NW), both in Westmount, surfaced by gpt. I fetched both PDFs on 2026-09-01. Hardisty: 'George Smiley, an auditor with the Hudson's Bay Company, moved into the home in 1925 and remained there until 1928'; designated a Municipal Historic Resource through Bylaw 20867 in March 2025. Griffith: 'occupied in 1924 by James B. Griffith, who lived at the residence until 1928'; Westmount 'is noted for its large collection of single detached homes, that were built between 1911 and 1925'. These are named, dated, City-published occupancy records spanning 1926-09-02, stronger for the exact-date variant than the directory OCR I relied on.

The City's 2021 Net Residential Density Annual Report (surfaced by gpt) contains built-outcome figures I did not use in round 1: the median built density of RF1 Single Detached Residential Zones in the redeveloping area was 19 du/nrha in 2021, the RF1 bar in the zone chart reads 17, and the mature planning districts Whitemud, Jasper Place, West Edmonton and Northwest are at 23 to 25 du/nrha, all from tax assessment, civic addressing and permit data with net residential land defined as excluding open space and road right-of-way. This is a matched-denominator built-density measurement for the end of the window, which my 2023 citation (32 du/nrha overall) did not isolate.

The same 2021 report's neighbourhood table (ID, planned density, 2021 built density) lets gpt's count of twelve developing neighbourhoods with planned density at or below 25 du/nrha be checked. I read the table and get the same twelve: Canossa 18, Carlton 21, Klarvatten 24, Hollick-Kenyon 22, Hudson 23, Ellerslie 18, Windermere 24, Richford 21, Blackmud Creek 25, Breckenridge Greens 25, Cameron Heights 24, Kinglet Gardens 19. The report notes that developing neighbourhoods with repealed NSPs were excluded from the list, so twelve is a floor for the developing area.

The City's Inglewood Neighbourhood Profile (surfaced by gpt) says 'Part of the area was annexed to Edmonton in 1904 and the remainder was annexed in 1920' and that Inglewood 'developed as a low density residential neighbourhood until the 1950s'. The 1920 annexation date conflicts with the City historical population table I used in round 1, which lists no annexation between Calder (April 26, 1917) and Beverly (December 30, 1961). I now report the 1926 boundary as the 1917 limits with this unresolved discrepancy noted; it does not move Inglewood outside the 1926 boundary under either source.

The Starling NSP office consolidation (working URL on webdocs.edmonton.ca, March 2025 consolidation of Bylaw 15461 adopted August 23, 2010 as Big Lake Neighbourhood Two, renamed by Bylaw 15988 January 30, 2012) gives a complete worked example for the coverage rule: plan area 132.07 ha (Table 1), 58.4 ha residential, 46.23 ha LDR1 at 'approximately 25 units per ha', 1.34 ha LDR2, overall 'density in Starling is 33.6 units per net hectare', housing ratio '59% low density residential to 41% medium density residential'.

The Zoning Bylaw 20001 amendments page (surfaced by gpt) lists each amendment's approval and effective date. Bylaw 21474 was approved April 27, 2026 and took effect August 1, 2026 (it reduces the RS maximum height); Bylaw 21499 was approved May 26, 2026 and takes effect January 1, 2027. No listed amendment takes effect between August 1, 2026 and September 2, 2026, so the instrument in force on the freeze date is identifiable from the page.
errors_in_other_reviews: gemini, ldh-existed-century: the Library and Archives Canada '1926 Census of the Prairie Provinces' landing page is cited as 'legal-audited' evidence that 'Edmonton possessed established residential neighbourhoods with dwelling houses'. The page is a database search portal; it contains no such statement and no Edmonton dwelling figures, as gemini's own finding half-admits. The URL timed out for me on 2026-09-01; a 2024 Wayback snapshot exists. The citation does not say what the reviewer claims, and the source-type label is wrong.

gemini, ldh-existed-century: the limitation 'Public web sources do not provide' the needed records, and the High-confidence 'Not established' built on it, reflect a search that was not performed rather than evidence found. The 1926 Henderson's Edmonton City Directory is digitized on archive.org, the City publishes named occupancy records spanning 1926 (Hardisty and Griffith statements), and the City's 2021 density report supplies a threshold with a defined denominator. High confidence cannot rest on the absence of a search.

gemini, ldh-planned-around: the review stops at the 1933 bylaw and treats the 1926-1933 gap as decisive. It evaluates no instrument from E2 to E6, although neighbourhood structure plans and land use bylaw schedules are public dated instruments that state permitted forms, site areas and designated densities. That is overgeneralization from one era to a century-long proposition. The canadacommons.ca mirror of the City's History of Zoning report returned HTTP 403 for me and has no Wayback snapshot; the same report is on edmonton.ca. Grading a secondary description 'strong' also departs from the brief's instruction to confirm the 1933 bylaw from a primary source; the City's Resource Guide does confirm bylaw number 26 and October 10, 1933.

gemini, both claims: the MATERIAL FRAMING CONCERN asserts the operationalization 'predetermines' failure. It does not. The 2021 report shows the built-outcome rule can be met at the end of the window from City data, and NSPs state designated densities per net residential hectare. The rule is hard for 1926, not impossible, and the brief already allows the calendar-year and exact-date variants to be reported separately.

gpt, ldh-planned-around, Starling: the claim that Starling is 'one direct example exceeding the 50 percent coverage rule using residential land as denominator' substitutes the wrong denominator. The brief's 50 percent rule is the share of the neighbourhood's land area, not of its residential land. Starling's plan area is 132.07 ha (Table 1, stamped Bylaw 15988), so LDR1 at 46.23 ha covers 35.0 percent, and LDR1 plus LDR2 (1.34 ha) covers 36.0 percent. Under the brief's rule Starling is a below-50-percent partial-coverage case, and it contributes 0.35 under the area-weighted calculation. The plan also states an overall density of 33.6 units per net hectare, above the 25 du/nrha threshold, and a 59 to 41 low to medium ratio. gpt's URL for the plan redirects to the City's page-not-found page; the working copy is https://webdocs.edmonton.ca/infraplan/plans_in_effect/Starling_NSP_Consolidation.pdf.

gpt, ldh-planned-around, 2014 Low Density Residential Lot Registrations report: the cited URL redirects to the City's page-not-found page and the Wayback Machine holds no snapshot, so the figures 83 neighbourhoods in ASPs, 73 with NSPs, 40 under development, 33 at 95 to 100 percent complete and 91,516 lots could not be verified by me. The City's 2021 density report gives a different frame that gpt also cites: 93 residential neighbourhoods categorized as developing, 70 under development, 55 with NSPs approved before 2010, and 16 with 95 to 100 percent low-density lot registration, 13 of which have repealed NSPs. I treat the 2014 figures as unverified and rely on the 2021 report.

gpt, ldh-existed-century: the City warning that 'Henderson's may not list every occupant' is graded a 'strong' challenging item. Directory omissions can only undercount occupied dwellings. They cannot challenge a finding that occupied housing existed, and they cut the other way for any density estimate built on the directory. The item belongs among limitations, not challenging evidence.

gpt, both claims: the MATERIAL FRAMING CONCERN that the 2026-09-02 endpoint 'cannot be observed' one day early is overstated for the instrument-in-force question. The amendments page lists effective dates for every amendment, including one taking effect January 1, 2027; nothing takes effect on September 2, 2026. Charter Bylaw 20001 as amended through Bylaw 21474 (effective August 1, 2026) is the instrument in force on the freeze date. For built stock, a one-day gap after a century of evidence is not a material uncertainty.

gpt, ldh-planned-around: the count of twelve neighbourhoods at or below 25 du/nrha is correct (I re-derived it from the report table), but two of the twelve (Blackmud Creek and Breckenridge Greens) sit exactly at 25, so the count is 10 under a strict below-25 reading; gpt should have stated the inclusive boundary. The count also uses whole-neighbourhood planned density, which gpt correctly flags as not the brief's permitted-development rule.

claims.proposition_evaluated: Documented, occupied low-density housing existed inside Edmonton's boundary in force in 1926 (tested at 1926-09-02 and for calendar year 1926), classified under the built-outcome rule in dwellings per hectare with a matched denominator, and remained part of the housing stock through 2026-09-02.
claims.interpretation_notes: Position unchanged from round 1: Partially supported. What is established: occupied detached houses inside the 1917 boundary on 1926-09-02 and throughout 1926 (Hardisty 1925-1928 and Griffith 1924-1928 in Westmount, the 1926 Henderson's directory householder entries, Highlands houses occupied from 1912), and low-density built outcome at the end of the window under a matched-denominator threshold (RF1 median 19 du/nrha in 2021 against the City's 25 du/nrha band, both on net residential land). What is not established: a dwellings-per-hectare figure for any 1926 area with a stated denominator and boundary. The gross-area bounds I computed in round 1 run the wrong way (net area is smaller than gross, so a low gross density does not bound net density below the threshold), and I do not use them to classify. Exact-date and calendar-year variants give the same result. Under T1 (25 du/nrha) and T2 (30 du/nrha) the end-of-window result is the same. The 1926 boundary is the 1917 boundary per the City population table; the Inglewood profile's 1920 annexation reference is an unresolved discrepancy that does not affect any area used here. I do not join gemini's framing concern: the rule is demanding for 1926 but the brief already separates existence from classification, and I report both. I do not join gpt's future-endpoint concern for the reason given in errors_in_other_reviews.

limitations: No source consulted gives, for any 1926 area, dwellings in use, net residential land area and a boundary together, so no 1926 dwellings-per-hectare figure is reported and the built-outcome classification for 1926 is not made.

Thresholds used: T1 25 du/nrha (Ellerslie NSP 2001 and the City's 2021 and 2023 density reports, net residential land); T2 30 du/nrha (2023 report map classes). Both are modern City measures applied to the whole window; no 1926-era threshold exists.

The gross-area bounds computed in round 1 (for example Glenora 1,546 dwellings on 1.63 km2 gross in 2012) cannot classify: net residential area is smaller than gross area, so a low gross density does not place net density below a net threshold.
The 2021 RF1 median is a median across zoned parcels in the redeveloping area, not a figure for a named 1926 neighbourhood.
The 1926 boundary is taken as the 1917 boundary from the City population table; the Inglewood profile's reference to a 1920 annexation is unreconciled.
unknowns: Dwellings per net residential hectare for Westmount, Highlands, Glenora or Inglewood in 1926.

what_would_change_my_verdict: A 1926 matched-denominator density at or below 25 du/nrha for any occupied area inside the 1917 boundary would move the verdict to Supported.

Evidence that no occupied area in 1926 was at or below the threshold, or that low-density stock disappeared city-wide at some point in the window, would move it toward Contradicted; neither is plausible on the record.
claims.suggested_one_line: Occupied detached houses inside Edmonton's 1917 boundary are documented on 2 September 1926 and throughout that year, and low-density built stock is measured at the end of the window, but no 1926 density figure with a matched denominator exists to complete the brief's classification.
claims.suggested_short_answer: Edmonton had occupied detached housing in 1926: City heritage records name residents of Westmount houses from 1924 and 1925 to 1928, the 1926 city directory lists householders across the city, and Highlands houses had been occupied since 1912. The City's own 2021 density report measures the median built density of its single-detached zones at 19 dwellings per net residential hectare, under its 25 threshold, so low-density stock is documented at the end of the window too. What nobody has published is a 1926 dwellings-per-hectare figure for any neighbourhood, so the strict classification for 1926 remains uncomputed.
suggested_tldr: Named Westmount houses were occupied across 2 September 1926.
Single-detached zones measured 19 dwellings per net residential hectare in 2021, below the City's 25 band.
No 1926 density figure with a matched denominator has been published.

claims.proposition_evaluated: Many neighbourhoods inside Edmonton's boundary in force in each era were planned around low-density housing, tested under the permitted-development rule, each era's terminology, the count and share readings of 'many' with both cutoffs, both neighbourhood units, both coverage calculations, both then-existing denominators, and both aggregation readings.
claims.interpretation_notes: Position unchanged from round 1: Partially supported. Eras used: E0 pre-zoning to October 10, 1933 (Bylaw 35 of 1923 and Bylaw 30 of 1925 as partial instruments); E1 Zoning Bylaw 26, 1933 to 1950; E2 Interim Development Bylaw 1339, 1950 to 1959; E3 Bylaw 1988 (1959) and Zoning Bylaw 2135 (1961-64) to 1980; E4 Land Use Bylaw 5996, July 3, 1980 to June 13, 2001; E5 Zoning Bylaw 12800, June 14, 2001 to December 31, 2023; E6 Charter Bylaw 20001, January 1, 2024 to 2026-09-02. Results by variant. Count reading, cumulative, plan-designation variant (NSPs and neighbourhood plans designating LDR land at 25 du/nrha or whole-neighbourhood planned density at or below 25 du/nrha): at least 12 developing-area neighbourhoods on the 2021 list plus Highlands (1985 plan) plus Ellerslie, all Edmonton instruments adopted after the 1982 annexation, so the count exceeds both cutoffs (10 and 5). Count reading under the strict permitted-development rule computed from zoning schedules: the 1980-2001 RF1 permitted 27.8 du/ha of site area (360 m2 per dwelling), above T1 and below T2, so E4 and E5 pass only under T2 (borderline: suites discretionary); the 1933 B district's minimum lot area was not found so E1 is uncomputed; the 2024 RS zone permits 133.3 du/ha and fails both thresholds, so the end-of-window instrument variant is Contradicted. E0 count is 3 (Glenora, Groat Estate, Highlands), below both cutoffs. Share reading: then-existing denominators per era were not computed under either denominator or either unit, so no share verdict is issued; against the present-day 375 developed neighbourhoods, 14 is 3.7 percent, far below 25 percent, but that denominator is the wrong one for cumulative testing. Coverage: the only neighbourhood with a computed covered share is Starling, LDR1 at 35.0 percent of plan area, which fails the 50 percent rule and counts 0.35 area-weighted; the count of below-50-percent partial coverage cases is at least 1 and the true number is unknown. Contemporaneous-unit boundaries are recoverable only for E0 subdivisions and post-1980 NSPs. The proposition as a whole is therefore Partially supported: the count reading is met cumulatively on plan designations, is threshold-dependent on zoning schedules, and fails at the end of the window; the share and coverage variants are not established. I keep this against gemini's Not established because gemini evaluated no post-1933 instrument, and I keep it against gpt's reliance on the unverifiable 2014 report and the mis-denominated Starling coverage figure.

limitations: Permitted densities are computed on site area from minimum site area per dwelling (RF1 1980-2001: 27.8 du/ha; RS 2024: 133.3 du/ha), while T1 and T2 are defined on net residential land. Site area is a subset of net residential land, so a site-area density above a net threshold is conservative in one direction only; where an instrument passes on site area it would pass on net area too.

Borderline instruments: RF1 1980-2001 (suites and semi-detached discretionary on abutting lots) treated as 1 dwelling per 360 m2, excluded variant 27.8 du/ha, included variant 55.6 du/ha; RF1 2017-2023 (suites permitted) counted with and without suites; Bylaw 26 B district uncomputed for want of the schedule. Count of borderline instruments: 3.
The neighbourhood-plan count uses whole-plan designated densities and LDR designations per net residential hectare, which is the plan's own measure rather than a zoning schedule's permitted maximum.

Then-existing denominators under either unit were not computed for any era, so no share-reading verdict is issued. The present-day count of 375 developed neighbourhoods is reported for orientation only.
Covered shares were computed for one neighbourhood (Starling). The count of neighbourhoods with coverage below 50 percent is at least 1 and otherwise unknown.
Contemporaneous planning-unit boundaries are recoverable for E0 subdivisions and post-1980 NSPs, not for E1 to E3.
gpt's 2014 lot registrations report could not be retrieved (dead link, no archive), so its figures are not used.

City boundaries per era are taken from the City population table and a secondary annexation compilation; the 1959 History of Annexations map (EAM-529) was not read. All developing-area plans cited were adopted by Edmonton after the January 1, 1982 annexation, so none is pre-annexation planning.

claims.suggested_one_line: Edmonton's own plans designated low-density land in more than ten neighbourhoods and its 1933 and 1980 bylaws zoned most lots for one house each, but the zone in force in 2026 permits eight dwellings per lot, and the share and coverage tests the brief requires cannot be run from public maps.
claims.suggested_short_answer: Yes for some readings, no for others. Counting neighbourhood plans, at least twelve developing neighbourhoods carry City-approved plans at or below 25 dwellings per net residential hectare, and Highlands and Ellerslie have plans saying low density in their own words, so 'many' is met on the count reading cumulatively. Before 1933 the record shows three covenanted or developer-controlled subdivisions, not many. The single-detached zone of 1980 to 2001 permitted 27.8 dwellings per hectare of site area, which is low density under a 30 threshold but not under 25. The zone in force in 2026 permits up to eight dwellings on a lot, or 133 per hectare, and is not low density under any threshold used. Whether a quarter of then-existing neighbourhoods were covered in any era could not be computed, because the historical zoning maps are not online.
suggested_tldr: At least twelve neighbourhood plans designate low-density housing at or below 25 dwellings per net hectare; count reading met cumulatively.
Pre-1933 deliberate planning is documented for three subdivisions only.
The 2026 zone permits eight dwellings per lot; the end-of-window instrument is not low density.
Share and coverage tests are uncomputed for want of historical maps.
